literal: When the Later Lord abdicated the throne to the crown prince, Sun Zhengyan whispered to someone, saying, "During the Wuding era I served as clerical officer at Guangzhou[9]; I heard Cao Puyan of Xiangcheng say: 'Among the sons of King Gao, the one called Abao will become emperor; when it reaches Dezhi and Chengzhi, the house will perish.'
idiomatic: When the Later Lord yielded the throne to the crown prince, Sun Zhengyan confided to someone: "In the Wuding era I was a clerical officer at Guangzhou[9]. I heard Cao Puyan of Xiangcheng prophesy: 'Of King Gao's sons, Abao will wear the crown; by the time of Dezhi and Chengzhi, the line will end.'"

literal: 'Abao' refers to the Tianbao era, 'Dezhi' to Dechang, and 'Chengzhi' to the Later Lord's era name Chengguang—and in the end his words proved true.'"
idiomatic: 'Abao' meant the Tianbao reign, 'Dezhi' meant Dechang, and 'Chengzhi' meant the Later Lord's Chengguang era—and in the end every word came true."

literal: Prince Shaoxin of Yuyang was the sixth son of Wenxiang.
idiomatic: Prince Shaoxin of Yuyang was the sixth son of Gao Cheng.

literal: He held in succession the ranks of special eminence, opener of the government, director of the central guard, protector of the army, and governor of Qing Province.
idiomatic: He rose through special eminence, opener of the government, director of the central guard, protector of the army, and governor of Qing Province.

literal: Passing through Yuyang, he sat together with the great merchant Zhong Changming to pray.
idiomatic: On the road through Yuyang he sat at prayer with the wealthy merchant Zhong Changming.

literal: When Prefect Zheng Daogai came to pay respects, Changming wished to rise; Shaoxin would not allow it and said, "What kind of low creature is this, that the master of the house should rise for him?
idiomatic: When Prefect Zheng Daogai came to pay his respects, Changming started to rise; Shaoxin stopped him and said, "What sort of wretch is this, that the host should stand for him?

literal: " He then made sworn brothers with Changming; his consort and Changming's wife became sworn sisters. He demanded gifts from the whole family, young and old alike, and the Zhong clan was ruined by it.
idiomatic: " He then swore brotherhood with Changming; his consort and Changming's wife became sworn sisters. He extorted gifts from every member of the household, young and old, until the Zhong family was beggared.

literal: When Qi perished he died at Chang'an.
idiomatic: When Qi fell he died at Chang'an.

literal: Book of Northern Qi, juan 11: This juan was originally missing; later hands supplemented it from the section on Wenxiang's sons in Beishi, juan 52, Biographies of Princes of the Imperial Clan of Qi.
idiomatic: Book of Northern Qi, juan 11: This juan was originally lost; later editors restored it from the account of Wenxiang's sons in Beishi, juan 52, Biographies of Princes of the Imperial Clan of Qi.

literal: The Song collator's note at the end of the juan in the editions of the Three Dynasties and the Southern edition reads: "This juan is identical to the Beishi."
idiomatic: At the end of the juan, the Song-era collation note in the Three Dynasties and Southern editions reads: "This juan matches the Beishi."

literal: On "set for the fifth day of the first month": in various editions "month" reads "daybreak."
idiomatic: On "set for the fifth day of the first month": various editions read daybreak for month.

literal: Beishi juan 52 and Cefu yuangui, juan 286, pp. 3368, read "month."
idiomatic: Beishi juan 52 and Cefu yuangui, juan 286, p. 3368, read month.

literal: "Fifth daybreak" makes no sense; emended per Beishi.
idiomatic: "Fifth daybreak" is impossible; emended per Beishi.

literal: On "At night there was divine light; Zhaoxuan Director Fashun requested that it be reported": in various editions "Zhaoxuan" reads as the two characters "Zhaoshi"; Beishi juan 52 has "Zhao" alone.
idiomatic: On "At night there was divine light; Zhaoxuan Director Fashun asked that it be reported to the throne": various editions read the two characters Zhaoshi for Zhaoxuan; Beishi juan 52 has Zhao alone.

literal: According to the Buddhist and Daoist Treatise in Weishu juan 114 and the Offices Treatise of Suishu juan 27, the office overseeing Buddhism in late Wei and early Qi was called Zhaoxuan; Northern Qi appointed one grand director and one director.
idiomatic: Weishu juan 114, Treatise on Buddhism and Daoism, and Suishu juan 27, Treatise on Offices, show that the agency governing Buddhism in late Wei and early Qi was called Zhaoxuan; Northern Qi placed one grand director and one director over it.

literal: The grand director of Zhaoxuan was also called Director of Zhaoxuan; the Beishi biography of Cui Xian, juan 32, mentions Director of Zhaoxuan Fashang; the supplementary biography of Du Bi in this book, juan 24, mentions Director of Zhaoxuan Sengda.
idiomatic: The grand director of Zhaoxuan was also styled Director of Zhaoxuan; Beishi juan 32, biography of Cui Xian, names Director of Zhaoxuan Fashang, and this book's supplementary biography of Du Bi, juan 24, names Director of Zhaoxuan Sengda.

literal: The Beishi wrongly wrote "Zhao" as "Zhao (illuminate)"; the person who supplemented this biography, finding it unintelligible, added the character "shi" without warrant—now corrected.
idiomatic: Beishi corrupted Zhao into the homophone for "illuminate"; the restorer of this biography, unable to make sense of it, added shi without cause—now corrected.

literal: On "Defeat at Mangshan": Cefu yuangui juan 218, p. 2616, reads "battle" for "defeat"; Tongzhi juan 85, Biographies of the Northern Qi Imperial Clan, reads "campaign."
idiomatic: On "Defeat at Mangshan": Cefu yuangui juan 218, p. 2616, reads battle for defeat; Tongzhi juan 85, Biographies of the Northern Qi Imperial Clan, reads campaign.

literal: In the third year of Heqing, 564, Northern Qi won the battle at Mangshan; see the biographies of Duan Shao in this book juan 16 and Hu Lüguang in juan 17. The passage below also speaks of a "great victory"—here "defeat" must be erroneous.
idiomatic: In the third year of Heqing, 564, Northern Qi won at Mangshan; see the biographies of Duan Shao in juan 16 and Hu Lüguang in juan 17 of this book. The lines below also speak of a "great victory"—defeat here must be wrong.

literal: On "When campaigning against Ding, Yang Shishen was in the army": in various editions the character "zhou" appears after "Ding"; Beishi omits it.
idiomatic: On "When campaigning against Ding, Yang Shishen was in the army": various editions insert zhou after Ding; Beishi does not.

literal: Ding Province belonged to Northern Qi, and nothing had changed in its status at this time—how could Gao Changgong, a prince of Northern Qi, have gone to attack it?
idiomatic: Ding Province was Northern Qi territory and had not changed hands—how could Gao Changgong, a prince of Qi, have marched against his own province?

literal: Above it already says Changgong and Duan Shao attacked Dingyang; this passage refers to exactly that affair.
idiomatic: Above, Changgong and Duan Shao are already said to have attacked Dingyang; this line refers to that same campaign.

literal: Later readers joined "Yang Shishen" to "Ding" and rashly added "zhou"; now deleted per Beishi.
idiomatic: Later readers read Yang Shishen as attached to Ding and added zhou without warrant; now deleted per Beishi.

literal: On "Again they heard the Zhou army had entered Sparrow-Mouse Gorge": in the editions of the Three Dynasties, Southern, Northern, and Hall, "sparrow (que)" reads "Xun," that is, the character "diao."
idiomatic: On "Again they heard the Zhou army had entered Sparrow-Mouse Gorge": in the Three Dynasties, Southern, Northern, and Hall editions, que (sparrow) reads Xun—the character diao.

literal: The Jiju and Bureau editions read "run," which is not a proper character.
idiomatic: The Jiju and Bureau editions read run, which is not a valid character.

literal: According to Commentary on the Water Classic juan 6, Fen River, "It again flows south past Guanjue Ford," with a note: "A ford on the Fen, southwest of Jiexiu county; popularly called Sparrow-Mouse Gorge; the road is treacherous for several tens of li.
idiomatic: Commentary on the Water Classic, juan 6, Fen River: "It flows south again past Guanjue Ford," with a note: "A ford on the Fen southwest of Jiexiu county, commonly called Sparrow-Mouse Gorge—a narrow road for several tens of li."

literal: " The Comprehensive Mirror, juan 172, p. 5360, in recounting the Zhou army's pursuit of the Northern Qi emperor, Hu Guang's note cites Song Bai: "Southeast of Lingshi county are Gaobi Ridge, Sparrow-Mouse Gorge, and Fen River Pass—all fortified ground on the west bank of the Fen.
idiomatic: The Comprehensive Mirror, juan 172, p. 5360, recounting the Zhou pursuit of the Northern Qi emperor, cites Hu Guang's note on Song Bai: "Southeast of Lingshi county lie Gaobi Ridge, Sparrow-Mouse Gorge, and Fen River Pass—all strong points on the west bank of the Fen."

literal: " Sparrow-Mouse Gorge was the road the Zhou army had to take marching from Jizhou through Lingshi and Jiexiu toward Taiyuan; there is no such place as "Xun-Mouse Gorge"; now corrected.
idiomatic: Sparrow-Mouse Gorge was the route the Zhou army had to take from Jizhou through Lingshi and Jiexiu toward Taiyuan; no place called Xun-Mouse Gorge exists—now corrected.

literal: On "Prince of Shuyang and Aguzi": in various editions and Beishi juan 52 "Shu (沭)" reads "Shu (沐)"; the Bureau edition, Comprehensive Mirror juan 172 p. 5362, and Tongzhi juan 85, Biographies of the Northern Qi Imperial Clan, read "Shu (沭)."
idiomatic: On "Prince of Shuyang and Aguzi": various editions and Beishi juan 52 read Mu (沐) for Shu (沭); the Bureau edition, Comprehensive Mirror juan 172 p. 5362, and Tongzhi juan 85, Biographies of the Northern Qi Imperial Clan, read Shu (沭).

literal: Shuyang belonged to Donghai commandery; see Suishu juan 31, Treatise on Geography, part 2—now following the Bureau edition.
idiomatic: Shuyang lay in Donghai commandery; see Suishu juan 31, Treatise on Geography, part 2—now following the Bureau edition.

literal: On "Consort Li gathered his remains for burial": in various editions "consort (fei)" reads "Qi"; Beishi juan 52 reads "fei."
idiomatic: On "Consort Li gathered his remains for burial": various editions read Qi for consort (fei); Beishi juan 52 reads fei.

literal: The supplementary biography of Wei Shou in this book juan 37 and the Beishi biography of Li Xiaozhen, juan 33, both say Yanzong married the Li clan—"consort" is correct; emended accordingly.
idiomatic: The supplementary biography of Wei Shou in juan 37 of this book and the Beishi biography of Li Xiaozhen, juan 33, both say Yanzong married a woman of the Li clan—consort is correct; emended accordingly.

literal: On "During the Wuding era I served as Guangzhou clerical officer": in various editions "Wuding" reads "Baoding"; Beishi reads "Wuding."
idiomatic: On "During the Wuding era I served as Guangzhou clerical officer": various editions read Baoding for Wuding; Beishi reads Wuding.

literal: This same affair appears in the supplementary biography of Qimu Huaiwen in this book juan 49, which likewise reads "Wuding."
idiomatic: The same episode appears in the supplementary biography of Qimu Huaiwen in juan 49 of this book, which also reads Wuding.

literal: Baoding is an era name of Emperor Wu of Zhou—by that time Gao Yang had long been emperor, which does not agree with what follows about "the sons of King Gao."
idiomatic: Baoding is an era of Emperor Wu of Zhou—by then Gao Yang had long reigned, which cannot square with what follows about "the sons of King Gao."

literal: Now emended per Beishi.
idiomatic: Now emended per Beishi.
